newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Macquarie sees rates driving strong market.
newsitem.headline: Macquarie sees rates driving strong market.

text.p: Investment bank and broking house Macquarie Bank expected Australian financial markets to continue to trade strongly in the year ahead, buoyed by the effect of low and possibly even lower interest rates, the bank said on Monday.

Macquarie Bank, which earlier reported stronger than expected annual profits, also said it saw a reassessment by the Reserve Bank of Australia of its capital adequacy rules for market risk, increasing Macquarie's capital strength and raising the possibility of a capital return.
Macquarie Chairman David Clarke said the bank had no preference or immediate plans for either a share buy-back or an increased dividend payout ratio.

But Clarke said the bank's shareholders would eventually have to look at a potential capital return once the Reserve Bank changes raised its capital adequacy ratio above 16 percent from its 13.2 percent level as at March 31.

"There's every chance that we'd have to look at it (a capital return)," Clarke said, adding that Macquarie had previously had its capital adequacy ratio between 13 and 15 percent. He said, however, he did not have a preferred range.
Macquarie increased its dividend payout ratio policy to between 55 to 60 percent from about 40 percent two years ago.
Earlier, Macquarie reported a net profit of A$116.94 million for the year to March 31, up 25.4 percent from the previous year and representing a return on average shareholder funds of 25.2 percent.
Earnings per share rose to 74.9 cents per share from 61 cents per share.
Macquarie said the strong result was due in part to the favourable market conditions evident in 1996/97.
Macquarie Managing Director Allan Moss said these favourable conditions had continued so far into the current 1997/98 year.

"With interest rates continuing to be low and perhaps going down a little bit further, there's every prospect for a reasonably good year in equity markets and we're also seeing quite a good flow in corporate activity," he said.
Moss said there was always the prospect of a correction from current all time highs.
"But the low level of interest rates is a cause for continuing confidence in the outlook for securities markets," he said.
Moss repeated earlier comments that recent changes to franking rules in the May budget would have a minimal impact on profits and may reduce the bank's ability to fully frank its dividends from 1999.
"We do think that even from 1999 we will be able to frank our dividends at at least two thirds of our current franking level," he said.
Macquarie's dividends in 1996/97 was fully franked, compared with 90 percent franking in 1995/96.
Moss also said the current insider trading allegations against senior corporate advisory executive Simon Hannes had not affected Macquarie's advisory business.
He said Macquarie had 130 advisory mandates during 1996/97.

"Our perception is that flow of business was unaffected by the Hannes matter, because our clients recognise this matter relates to an individual and not the bank as a whole," Moss told a news conference.
"We would expect that our clients would continue to be similarly supportive in the currrent year," he said.
Hannes is alleged to bought options in transport group TNT Ltd just before Dutch postal and telecoms group KPN NV launched a surprise takeover bid.
Macquarie advised TNT on the takeover bid.
Hannes lawyers have said he would plead not guilty.
Macquarie's shares were up eight cents at A$9.54 at 12.25 p.m. (0225 GMT).
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
